The idea that individuals became more resistant and passed it on describes inheritance of acquired traits, which does not occur. The idea that the antibiotic induced mutations is contradicted by the note that no new mutations were detected.

items.stem: The nursery owner wants to explain why the resistance allele frequency rose in Greenhouse A. Which explanation best uses the concept of natural selection?

Individual aphids became resistant by surviving sprays and passed that acquired resistance to their offspring.
Aphids with the R genotype survived and reproduced more than others under weekly Bt-X, so R became more common in the next generations.
Bt-X exposure caused aphids to migrate away from Greenhouse A, which left the resistant ones behind by chance.
option_rationale: Misconception: the environment directs mutations toward need; mutations are random and exist before selection.
Misconception: Lamarckian inheritance of acquired traits; individuals do not change their genotype by surviving.
Correct: heritable variation plus differential survival and reproduction increases R frequency.
Misconception: attributes allele change to migration/drift; the table shows no migration and the population is large.
items.explanation_en: Resistance variation (allele R) already existed in the population at 0.10. Weekly Bt-X made RR aphids far more likely to survive and reproduce, so R rose from 0.10 to 0.60. The mutation-on-demand option is wrong because mutations are random and not caused by need. The acquired-resistance option is wrong because surviving a spray does not alter genotype or pass on a changed trait. The migration option is wrong because nothing in the data indicates migration, and large populations are not dominated by drift.

0.84; all carriers survive the dose, so selection on R is complete.

Misconception: confuses q^2 = 0.36 (RR) with carriers and treats Rr as surviving despite recessive resistance.
Misconception: counts RR+Rr (1-0.16) as survivors, ignoring that resistance is fully recessive.

The refuge will eliminate the R allele entirely, because natural selection always removes costly alleles from a population.
The refuge will have no effect, because resistance is recessive and allele frequencies cannot change without spraying.

Misconception: selection always eliminates a disfavored allele; heterozygotes shield it and it persists at low frequency.
Misconception: allele frequencies change only through the sprayed environment; the cost of resistance still selects against R.
items.explanation_en: In unsprayed Greenhouse C, RR aphids have 20% lower reproduction and R drifted from 0.10 to 0.09, so selection slightly disfavors R without sprays. The eliminate-entirely option is wrong because R persists in heterozygotes. The no-effect option ignores the fitness cost shown in the table.

Yes, a new species: resistance to Bt-X is a new adaptation, and any new adaptation means speciation has occurred.
Not a new species yet, but only because speciation requires many thousands of years, regardless of whether reproductive isolation is observed.

The option claiming all cells became resistant is contradicted by the 61% figure and by the non-directed nature of selection.

CAP-cAMP binds near the promoter and enhances RNA polymerase binding (positive control); it is active when cAMP is high, which occurs when glucose is low, and inactive when glucose is high.

rubric_rows.criterion: Repressor function and its control by inducer
CAP-cAMP function and its control by glucose
required_elements: active when glucose is low (cAMP high); inactive when glucose is high

parts.label: b

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct ratio with work
alt_solutions: (184-4)/4 = 45 as percent-style increase of 4500% or 45 times greater is accepted only if clearly stated

parts.label: c

payload.title: Abstract Monopolist: Graph, Profit, Surplus, and Deadweight Loss

stimulus.description: Linear market demand curve for a single-price monopolist with a horizontal marginal cost curve that equals average total cost. Axes: Quantity (units) 0 to 50, Price and cost (dollars) 0 to 100.

data.note: The firm is the only seller and charges one price to all buyers. MR is not drawn; students must derive and draw it.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Using the demand and cost information in the graph, draw a correctly labeled monopoly graph. Include D, MC = ATC, and the marginal revenue curve (MR), and label the profit-maximizing quantity Qm, the monopoly price Pm, and the point on the demand curve above Qm. Give the numerical values of the MR intercepts and of Qm and Pm.
parts.model_answer: MR = 100 - 4Q: vertical intercept 100, horizontal intercept 25, twice as steep as D. MR = MC: 100 - 4Q = 20 gives Qm = 20. Pm = 100 - 2(20) = 60, read from demand. Graph shows D, MC = ATC at 20, MR below D, Qm = 20 at the MR = MC intersection, and Pm = 60 on D directly above Qm.

rubric_rows.criterion: MR curve drawn from the same vertical intercept as D, downward sloping, twice as steep as D (horizontal intercept 25), labeled
D and horizontal MC = ATC at 20 drawn and labeled
Qm = 20 identified at the MR = MC intersection
Pm = 60 read from the demand curve above Qm, with dashed lines to the axes
required_elements: price from D not from MR or MC

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the monopolist's economic profit and shade and label the profit rectangle on your graph.
parts.model_answer: Profit = (Pm - ATC) x Qm = (60 - 20)(20) = $800. Shaded rectangle with height from 20 to 60 and width from 0 to 20.

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct profit calculation
Rectangle shaded between ATC = 20 and Pm = 60 from Q = 0 to Qm = 20 and labeled

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the deadweight loss caused by the monopoly relative to the perfectly competitive outcome, and shade and label it on your graph.
parts.model_answer: Competitive quantity: 100 - 2Q = 20 gives Q = 40. DWL = 1/2 x (40 - 20) x (60 - 20) = 1/2 x 20 x 40 = $400. Triangle with vertices (20,60), (20,20), (40,20).

rubric_rows.criterion: Correct DWL calculation using Qc = 40
Triangle shaded with vertices (20,60), (20,20), (40,20) and labeled DWL
required_elements: bounded by D, MC, and the vertical line at Qm

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The monopolist is now required to charge a single price equal to its marginal cost of $20. Calculate the change in consumer surplus compared with the unregulated monopoly outcome, and explain, using your numbers, why the change in consumer surplus is larger than the monopolist's profit change in absolute value.
parts.model_answer: Monopoly CS = 1/2 x 20 x (100 - 60) = $400. At P = 20, Q = 40, CS = 1/2 x 40 x 80 = $1,600. CS rises by $1,200. Profit falls by $800 (to zero), so consumers gain $1,200 while the firm loses $800; the extra $400 equals the DWL that is eliminated.

rubric_rows.criterion: Change in consumer surplus is +$1,200 (from $400 to $1,600)
Explains with numbers that the CS gain exceeds the $800 profit loss by $400 because the DWL is recovered

payload.design_note: Purely abstract linear demand and constant MC. The graph skill (4.A) is exercised by deriving and drawing MR, locating Qm and Pm, and shading the profit and DWL areas. MC=20

qc=sp.solve(sp.Eq(D,MC),Q)[0]

cs_m=sp.Rational(1,2)*qm*(100-pm)
cs_c=sp.Rational(1,2)*qc*(100-MC)
dcs=cs_c-cs_m

{"part":"c","pass":bool(qc==40 and dwl==400),"detail":str(dwl)},
